item.title: 6 Takeaways From the 2026 DealBook Summit
item.description:
The promise and peril of artificial intelligence, America’s shifting politics and what it means for businesses and global trade, the reverberations of Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia on Silicon Valley and Wall Street, and more dominated the discussions at the annual DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Over the course of the day, speakers, including Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, dug into A.I.’s growth (and security) challenges. There was also plenty of chatter about the speakers’ relationships with President Trump before and since Election Day, including from Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York.

There were quirkier moments, too. Polymarket’s chief executive, Shayne Coplan, said he had A.I. agents trading on his laptop in his green room as he spoke.

The annual summit, hosted by Andrew Ross Sorkin, founder of DealBook, has taken place since 2011.

Here are six main themes that emerged.

The morning started off with comments on the debate that has gripped Wall Street: Is the recent tech-stock sell-off a blip, or a sign the A.I. industry is doomed to run out of steam? Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, warned that while growth in A.I. had helped keep the global economy resilient, it might not end well. There is a “very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually,” she said.

On the flip side, Mr. Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, an A.I. powerhouse expected to go public as soon as next year, downplayed the “ups and downs of valuations.” Overall, he said, the “trend is going to be strong.”

The debate took on extra emphasis with Anthropic pricing a record-setting I.P.O. valuing the giant at more than $1.5 trillion. Its shares are set to begin trading on Thursday.

“These companies are remarkably consequential companies for the future of the economy, the future of society,” said Adena Friedman, chief executive of Nasdaq, whose stock exchange will list Anthropic’s shares.

Beyond the financial fears of how fast the A.I. industry is growing is a fear of how powerful the technology itself has become. Greg Brockman, a founder at OpenAI and its president, said A.I. safety had become a bigger conversation (and focus at his company) as models became more capable.

“Models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new,” he said. “And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift.”

Both he and Mr. Altman stressed the need for humans to retain a tight control of the technology. Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, for one, sounded skeptical that so-called alignment — the science of teaching A.I. to broadly follow human preferences and instructions — is fully possible.

Palmer Luckey, chief executive of defense behemoth Anduril, sees a potential dark cloud, however. He said he believe the recent wave of tech outages bedeviling airlines, banks and our digital lives had an A.I. angle. He blamed attackers using A.I. tools to target outdated infrastructure.

“As of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast-moving in using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” he said.

Mayor Mamdani of New York City explained a bit about how he maintains an amicable relationship with President Trump. Mr. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, said the key to dealing with the president was “to focus on any possible area of commonality — and the reason for that is the stakes are so immense.”

He gave the example of how he called the president to plead his case, asking for a relaxation of rules to help the city’s bodegas and small retailers meet new federal food-stocking rules

Prime Minister Carney of Canada who met with Mr. Trump earlier in the day on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, has found negotiations on the countries’ trade spat progressing slower than he’d like.

But he also offered a paradoxical view. In certain settings, Mr. Trump comes across as personable and engaged.

“He listens a lot more in private,” Mr. Carney said. “I mean, he’s interested, genuinely, in your opinion, and it’s a reasonably direct conversation.” Even so, Canada is advancing trade ties with China while talks with the Trump administration remain stalled over their tit-for-tat tariff war.

Governance watchdogs have long called into question business figures’ close ties to the president and his family — an issue that could draw serious scrutiny from a Democrat-controlled congress.

David Ellison, chief executive of Skydance, could be one under the political microscope. In conversation with Mr. Sorkin, Mr. Ellison took on issues as big as press freedom and as small as Rush Hour 4. Skydance’s decision to greenlight production of the film was for creative and commercial reasons, Mr. Ellison said, not because the studio was pressured to do so by Mr. Trump, who was previously reported to have requested the studio to revive the franchise.

Mr. Ellison’s media conglomerate, Paramount Skydance, was born out of a mega merger with Warner Bros. after the Justice Department this summer shuttered its investigation into the deal. Mr. Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, has a close relationship with Mr. Trump.

“We’ve been fortunate enough to be able to work closely with this administration,” Mr. Ellison said. But, he added, “when we started the Paramount deal, that was under the Biden administration” with whom “we were working very closely.”

Later in the day, Mr. Coplan of Polymarket defended his company’s ties to Donald Trump Jr., the president’s oldest son, who’s an investor in the company via his venture firm 1789 Capital, saying the relationship is “heavily overblown.”

The tech bosses on the agenda — Mr. Altman, Mr. Luckey of Anduril and Mr. Nadella of Microsoft — all expressed empathy toward Mr. Huang’s predicament after his ouster last week from Nvidia after reports of his affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese asset.

Some in the Trump administration have suggested Nvidia’s parting with Mr. Huang, who has said he would like a shot to return to the chip making giant, is the right move. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that the company needed a “dramatic shake-up” — widely interpreted as a call for new blood to run Nvidia.

Tech leaders have had kinder words. Mr. Altman told Andrew Ross Sorkin: “I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

Mr. Musk, like others in Silicon Valley, said Mr. Huang was irreplaceable.

“Let’s say you’re the Chicago Bulls, middle of your second season, and you’ve got a winning streak that’s just going to happen, and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team,” Mr. Musk said, adding that “doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me.”

Prediction markets, platforms that allow users to wager on real-world events like election outcomes and sports, have taken financial markets by storm.

Traders on Polymarket, for example, can and have wagered on what speakers at the DealBook Summit would say. Such bets have drawn heavy scrutiny.

“Mention markets are entertaining, that’s for sure,” said Vlad Tenev, chief executive of Robinhood, whose company has banned such wagers. “But they’re also easy to manipulate.”

Mr. Coplan of Polymarket had a more charitable view about the rise of prediction markets in general, arguing it is giving rise to a new type of savvy investor.

“People have gravitated to that as an information source,” he said. “And that’s the thing that I’m really excited about.”

Some speakers also talked about being way too online.

Hailey Bieber, the entrepreneur who sold her Rhode beauty brand for at least $800 million last year, said she was “100 percent” a social media addict. She, too, feels insecure after looking at people online, she said.

“It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face. They make your lips bigger, your nose smaller,” she says. “That definitely can be harmful and misleading.”

item.title: One of Anthropic’s Biggest I.P.O. Winners Feels a Bit Uneasy About the Whole Thing
item.description:
Dustin Moskovitz was one of Anthropic’s earliest investors, and that bet is expected to be worth billions as the company goes public Thursday.

The moment seems to fill him with worry.

The 42-year-old billionaire made his fortune as co-founder of Facebook and has, for years, been both intrigued and troubled by the path of artificial intelligence. He donated to OpenAI early on only to fall out with the company’s leaders as it became more of a business.

Anthropic was supposed to be different. Founded by Dario Amodei and other OpenAI employees who were concerned that A.I. wasn’t being developed for the good of humanity, Anthropic’s priority would be A.I. safety. Mr. Moskovitz helped get it off the ground.

Mr. Moskovitz embodies a tension between free-market capitalism and A.I. safety at the heart of Anthropic’s initial public offering. In multiple posts on social media, he has expressed his worry that Anthropic — and A.I. — is advancing too quickly for society to control, just as Wall Street hands Anthropic more than $80 billion of additional firepower in the biggest I.P.O. ever.

In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Moskovitz established some distance from the company, where he served as a board observer, or a nonvoting board member.

“Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said, referring to his wife, Cari Tuna. “A.I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”

In an unusual move, the couple transferred their Anthropic stake — which would be worth billions of dollars today — into a nonprofit in early 2025 so that he and Ms. Tuna would not personally profit from selling the stock in the public market, a spokesman for the couple said. The spokesman, Mike Levine, declined to disclose the nonprofit.

Mr. Moskovitz, who is one of the country’s biggest Democratic donors, is also deeply involved in the effective altruist movement. He is the biggest funder of nonprofits devoted to A.I. safety — often led by early A.I. believers who are disturbed that stock market expectations will overpower safety concerns for leading A.I. companies like Anthropic. They see the potential dangers multiplying as A.I. systems improve rapidly, pointing to recent episodes of so-called A.I. “agents” coordinating their own cyberattacks outside of controlled environments.

Mr. Moskovitz’s unease has estranged him from close friends in Silicon Valley, like the Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg, his former Harvard University roommate, and it has made him a foil for rivals like SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, a frequent target of Mr. Moskovitz online.

Eric Ries, a former Anthropic adviser who helped the company set up a unique corporate structure, said the company had taken steps to insulate itself from some of the typical Wall Street pressures. But he knows his friend, Mr. Moskovitz, still worries.

“This is the one time when it’s been bad for someone to have invested early and called their shot and gotten it right,” said Mr. Ries, who advises Silicon Valley companies about management practices. Mr. Moskovitz, he added, appears to feel a sense of his place in history, which creates a “tremendous pressure and responsibility to get it right.”

Mr. Moskovitz, who declined to be interviewed for this article and makes few public appearances, has given the clearest expression of how he feels on the liberal-leaning social network Bluesky, where he gleefully debates his critics, offers candid anecdotes about and takedowns of fellow Silicon Valley titans, and occasionally discloses inside-the-boardroom information about Anthropic.

Mr. Moskovitz has christened himself an “ ‘overly online’ board observer.” Some of Mr. Moskovitz’s allies have been alarmed by his level of frankness on the platform.

In April, for instance, Mr. Moskovitz wrote that he felt Anthropic going public was “problematic” and that he had “tried to advise them to delay.”

By September, Mr. Moskovitz’s tone had turned sardonic. He recapped recent A.I. developments — cybersecurity failures, claims of potential human extinction, A.I. agents escaping sandboxes — landing on a dose of dark humor about the multitrillion-dollar valuation Anthropic could command when it starts publicly trading: “And one $2T IPO is proceeding as scheduled.”

Mr. Moskovitz and Dr. Amodei had known each other long before Anthropic’s founding. They were part of a social circle interested in effective altruism, the brainy, tech-inflected approach to philanthropy that uses data-driven evidence to inform decision-making.

They met through Holden Karnofsky, who helped create Open Philanthropy, Mr. Moskovitz’s effective-altruistic organization. Mr. Karnofsky was dating, and later married, Daniela Amodei, Dario’s sister. Dr. Amodei once joined Mr. Moskovitz at Burning Man, the desert festival popular with the tech crowd, according to a person who knows Mr. Moskovitz.

Dr. Amodei had just joined OpenAI, then a small San Francisco-based research lab that operated as a nonprofit when he helped arrange for Open Philanthropy, now called Coefficient Giving, to donate $30 million to OpenAI in 2017. Mr. Moskovitz said he saw the deal as a way to give Mr. Karnofsky a seat on its board and push the company in a safety direction. “If they have a bad approach now, that’s all the more reason to get involved,” Mr. Moskovitz wrote Mr. Karnofsky in late 2016, according to an email he has shared.

Mr. Moskovitz later said that strategy didn’t work — and that he was “most gullible” for backing OpenAI.

Over time, Dr. Amodei became more vocal inside OpenAI about the potential harms from A.I., and in 2020, he and his sister, who also worked at OpenAI, along with five of their colleagues, left the company to start Anthropic. They set it up as a for-profit company with an untypical legal structure — a public benefit corporation that would lessen the influence of outside shareholders.

The group struggled to win the backing of traditional venture capitalists, which it needed in the expensive business of developing A.I. models. Then Mr. Moskovitz came along. He invested $15 million to $25 million of the $124 million Anthropic raised overall in its first round of funding in 2021, according to two people familiar with the funding round.

Earlier this year, Mr. Moskovitz said in a post that his goal in funding the company was to extricate the founders from OpenAI and “create a race to the top (of ethics) by having a real safety lab at the frontier.” He added, without apparent irony, that his funding of Anthropic “might well be an action that ended the world.”

Mr. Moskovitz was one of the few people in Anthropic’s board room with extensive business credentials in the company’s early years. He had spent years running Asana, a workplace software company he founded, which had gone public in 2020, and was valued at roughly $25 billion at its height.

At times, he pressed executives on standard commercial issues, such as how they would get the company’s A.I. chatbot, Claude, into the hands of more corporate customers, a person close to Anthropic said.

Other times, he asked for specific plans about the security and safety of its models, said a person who attended one of those board meetings.

Meanwhile, Mr. Moskovitz was putting more and more money into A.I. safety projects, through both effective altruism and Democratic politics. Mr. Moskovitz and Ms. Tuna have donated over $8 billion to charity. In April, Mr. Moskovitz said he had committed about $20 billion more to charitable efforts, which includes the Anthropic stake. Most of the couple’s funding has gone toward global-health efforts like disease prevention, as well as to A.I. safety nonprofits.

And over the last decade, Mr. Moskovitz has achieved first-name-only-required status in Democratic circles, meeting privately with President Joseph Biden Jr. to talk about A.I. safety and donating about $140 million to liberal super PACs.

That has put him at odds with tech billionaires who have increasingly made a rightward tilt. Mr. Moskovitz has squabbled online with Marc Andreessen, who serves on the board of Meta and was one of Asana’s first investors and who has allied himself with the Trump administration’s freewheeling position on A.I. development.

Mr. Moskovitz has at times been consumed with blasting Mr. Musk and Tesla, which he once called an Enron-like fraud. Not to be outdone, Mr. Musk retorted on social media that Mr. Moskovitz was “a pompous idiot.”

Mr. Moskovitz wrote and shared a five-page memo about why effective altruists should not work with Mr. Musk. One section, according to a Bluesky post, was titled “Elon is a Bad Person.”

Perhaps the most telling sign of Mr. Moskovitz’s disappointments with Silicon Valley has been the recent, surprising change of tone around the company that made him a billionaire in the first place: Facebook.

Mr. Moskovitz has long defended the company and Mr. Zuckerberg even as he excoriated the Valley. But in the last year, Mr. Moskovitz has sharply critiqued Mr. Zuckerberg and Meta, primarily for creating addiction and spreading misinformation ever since their decision to start News Feed, what he called the company’s “original sin.”

“I absolutely made these cases of harm to Zuck and other execs, many times,” he wrote in April. “I am very sorry for failing to stop the madness and every day I’m embarrassed to have helped it begin.”

Mr. Moskovitz wrote in May that he sold all of his remaining stake in the company and he did so “precisely because I don’t approve of the company’s actions.”

Mr. Zuckerberg is similarly privately frustrated with Mr. Moskovitz and his point of view on A.I., according to a person who has spoken to Mr. Zuckerberg about it.

After leaving Facebook, Mr. Moskovitz struggled at Asana with short-term shareholder pressures. As its stock price slid, he used his own money to buy shares and prove he still had faith in the company.

Mr. Moskovitz stepped down as Asana’s chief executive last year. Its market capitalization has fallen to about $2 billion.

Mr. Ries, who advised Mr. Moskovitz at Asana, said he thought the experience as a public company chief executive helped shape his views on Anthropic’s I.P.O. “He knows first hand the ways that markets puts pressure on mission-driven companies, ” Mr. Ries added, referring to Asana. “He’s seen this financial gravity up close and it hasn’t been pretty.”

In the run-up to the public offering, Mr. Moskovitz has expressed frustration that no one — not at Anthropic, not in politics — seems to be listening to him. Neither Dario nor Daniela Amodei has spoken to Mr. Moskovitz in over a year, said a person with knowledge of their conversations.

He said he no longer speaks to his once “close friends” Mr. Zuckerberg or Sam Altman, the OpenAI chief executive. Even Mr. Karnofsky, his longtime top aide who in 2024 left Open Philanthropy and now works at Anthropic in a technical role, basically does not have time for some of his complaints, Mr. Moskovitz wrote on Bluesky.

“What policymakers and politicians are listening to me? Where are they? I want to finally meet one,” he wrote last year. “Attempting to be heard is not the same as being listened to.”

item.title: Anthropic I.P.O. Highlights How Washington Has Fallen Behind
item.description:
When Anthropic begins to list its shares for public trading on Thursday, the first-of-its-kind offering will double as a watershed moment for a fast-budding technology that may someday revolutionize American life.

But it will also spotlight the ways in which artificial intelligence has outpaced the federal government’s ability to prepare — and the vast economic consequences that could soon follow because Washington acted too late.

Despite an increasingly anxious public, the Trump administration and its departing Republican majority in Congress have done little over the past two years to address or mitigate the potential hazards of A.I., including mass job losses. They have opted to cheerlead the arrival of new technology while largely ignoring its risks, an approach that has encouraged economic growth while leaving workers and businesses at the mercy of an unpredictable transformation.

It is a tension that Anthropic itself has acknowledged as it looks to woo investors in what could be the largest, most anticipated public offering in history. The company’s official prospectus portrays A.I. as cataclysmic for “every area of human endeavor,” from medical research to military warfare, and describes its own inventions as rife with “catastrophic or existential” danger to life itself.

While policymakers in Washington have prepared a series of bills that aim to confront those threats, many remain stuck in Congress. That includes proposals that would help address the economic consequences of A.I. by aiding displaced workers and bolstering the federal safety net.

Members of Congress have similarly been unable to enact measures intended to contain A.I. security threats or deal with its implications for health care, education, the energy grid or the tax code. Frequently, the Trump administration has portrayed some of the proposed limitations on A.I. as unnecessary, while shrugging off concerns that the industry itself could fall victim to a financially costly bubble.

Glenn Hubbard, an economist at Columbia Business School who served as a top adviser to President George W. Bush, said Anthropic’s public offering evinced a series of truths — that the company has been “highly successful” and that “Washington remains fairly unprepared” for what’s ahead.

He likened A.I. to the arrival of electricity, the combustion engine and mainframe computing — some of the many moments over the past century that helped to “reinvent” the U.S. economy. But, Mr. Hubbard added, those transformations did not always occur equally and simultaneously for everyone, a precedent that once again looms large entering a new chapter of the digital age.

“In general, where I would give the administration low marks is thinking about the speed of technological change that’s possible and getting ready for it,” he said.

For the moment, the focus is on the first day of trading for Anthropic, whose arrival on the Nasdaq coincides with a moment of heightened scrutiny around A.I. and its pioneers. As the first frontier lab to be listed publicly, its trajectory will be closely watched — touching off additional I.P.O.s and a wave of new investment if it succeeds, or perhaps setting off a chain reaction that upends the industry if it fails.

The stakes are just as great for the U.S. economy, at a time when the breakneck pace of A.I. investment is powering much of the nation’s growth and driving outsize gains in the stock market. If Anthropic falters, the nation’s prime source of economic strength could stumble along with it. That risk was apparent this week, as major indexes whipsawed in tandem with Nvidia, a chipmaker at the center of the A.I. ecosystem, after the ouster of its embattled chief executive. It also reported a sharp uptick in quarterly sales.

The result is a “financial pressure” on Anthropic, said Amos Toh, a senior counsel at the Brennan Center’s Liberty and National Security Program. But, he said, it faced a contradiction: Its business model is “conditioned on accelerating the development of the technology toward an end state” that Anthropic itself has acknowledged could be “potentially catastrophic.”

That, to Mr. Toh, raised the key question: “How will this tension play out in A.I. regulation and efforts by Congress to regulate the technology?”

So far, at least, those regulatory efforts have largely faltered.

By the Brennan Center’s count, Democrats and Republicans in Congress have unveiled 56 major bills over the past two years seeking to address some of the greatest A.I. risks. The measures are wide ranging, aiming to create new federal oversight agencies, establish new reporting requirements for cybersecurity incidents and even mandates for a “kill switch” allowing federal regulators to shut off rogue A.I. agents. Some, like the Frontier Act, which looks to manage catastrophic A.I. risks, have the support of Democrats and Republicans.

But despite the support, only one of those measures has become law in Republican-controlled Washington. It was narrowly focused on thwarting sexually explicit, A.I.-generated videos, known as “deepfakes.”

There are additional bills that would address the economic consequences: tracking A.I.-related layoffs, retraining affected workers and augmenting their wages if they are cast from their jobs by technology. Lawmakers including Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, have focused on the safety net, and others including Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont, have sought to award the public a portion of the wealth generated by the likes of Anthropic as they hit public markets.

But those, too, have gone nowhere, meaning the largest I.P.O. in history is set to occur even though the government “doesn’t have the instruments to measure it, or the safety net to be prepared for what’s coming,” said Erik Brynjolfsson, a leading A.I. expert who heads the Stanford Digital Economy Lab.

Mr. Brynjolfsson’s organization has embarked on its own campaign to try to track the economic changes wrought by A.I. Its latest research, produced in conjunction with the payroll firm ADP, found continued evidence that young workers in A.I.-exposed industries were having a harder time finding employment.

It is a far cry from the projections that millions of workers could someday lose their jobs from wide-scale A.I. adoption, but Mr. Brynjolfsson said the correlation was instructive in a key respect: “A.I. is starting to accelerate its own development sooner than Washington has assumed.”

The inaction on Capitol Hill fanned anger among Democrats on the eve of the Anthropic public offering. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who leads her party on the banking committee, expressed alarm in a statement about the “threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this I.P.O. goes awry.” She said the Trump administration was “asleep at the switch.”

Voters appeared to echo some of that unease in this year’s elections, as they opted to restrict A.I. in dozens of ballot measures and topple candidates viewed as too friendly to the industry. Already, incoming Democratic leaders have promised an aggressive crackdown, including new moratoriums on data centers, which many communities have blamed for increasing pollution and rising utility prices.

“We haven’t seen the action to date yet, but I think there’s a growing appetite to act,” said Asad Ramzanali, the director of artificial intelligence and technology policy at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, adding that for the “first time it feels like there’s momentum.”

But Democrats may face a potential obstacle in President Trump, who has likened data centers to “GOLD” on social media and broadly looked to court what he sees as the vast “riches” of A.I. He has resisted calls for any slowdown and celebrated the soaring stock returns of major technology companies, which he has chalked up to his administration’s hands-off policies.

The White House did not respond to multiple requests for comments.

Some investors and economists fear that the most significant lapse in Washington is an inattentiveness to the financing tactics powering A.I. development. To build new data centers and ramp up the technology, many companies are borrowing and spending staggering sums, raising the possibility that they may never earn enough revenue or attract enough customers to justify all of the investment.

Ben Harris, the vice president and director of economic studies at the Brookings Institution, said there was “not enough attention being paid” to these practices in Washington.

“A.I. could still be profitable, and we could still have massive stability risk, because it’s not as profitable as those who invested in it thought,” he said.

Among the biggest A.I. critics, there is even a fear that inadequate regulation could precipitate the sort of meltdown last seen during the global financial crisis, which could wreak havoc on workers’ retirement savings. But the Trump administration has rejected those fears as well, and in advance of the Anthropic public offering, it has repeatedly rebuffed calls for an intervention.

Such a situation unfolded in November as investors grew troubled over companies including Alphabet and Meta, and the scale of their A.I. spending. Despite a market rout, Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, pointed that month to what he described as a “well-financed ecosystem.”

Mr. Hassett added in an appearance on CNBC that there were “five or six J.P. Morgans that could come in and swoop around and clean things up if need be.”

While he then predicted that would not be necessary, Mr. Hassett still added of the industry: “I don’t think that there’s a risk of a wholesale sell-off at all.”

item.title: Iran Keeps Up Unrelenting Attacks on Ships in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Iran has kept up its unrelenting attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, including one this week on a tanker that sustained two hits and left one sailor missing.

So far this month, according to official reports and analysts who track the activity in the region, there have been at least 19 attacks on ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway that had carried one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

But the assault late Monday night on a disabled tanker has raised new alarms in the shipping industry.

After the vessel, the Tara Gas, was struck once, Iran issued warnings to salvage tugboats providing assistance, said Dimitris Maniatis, the chief executive of Marisks, a maritime risk consultancy. A second attack forced the crew of the Tara Gas to abandon the ship, he said.

The double attack put emergency workers and towing vessels, at risk. Throughout the war, Iran has used attacks to try to force shippers to comply with its claim to control navigation in the strait. Most of the strikes have been single hits that often disable vessels. At least 27 seafarers have been killed and 32 injured, according to official tallies and reporting by The New York Times. At least five sailors are missing.

“The incident may indicate a deliberate effort to extend the effects of an initial attack by discouraging or preventing rescue, recovery and salvage operations,” Mr. Maniatis said. Vessels carrying gas or other hazardous material would be particularly vulnerable.

The Tara Gas, which was carrying liquefied petroleum gas, was struck by an unidentified projectile that caused a fire in the engine room. The vessel issued a distress alert, according to several maritime risk firms.

Initial reports indicated that the crew members were safe.

The next day, however, the vessel was attacked a second time, resulting in a fire, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center, which is run by Britain’s Royal Navy.

Of the 25 crew members, all of whom were from India, one was reported missing and two were hospitalized with severe burns, according to Manoj Yadav, who leads the union representing Indian sailors.

The rest of the crew members were evacuated to Khasab, Oman, and search-and-rescue operations were continuing, Mr. Yadav said.

Sarbananda Sonowal, India’s minister of ports, shipping and waterways, said in a post on social media that the Indian government was coordinating with the ship management company and regional rescue authorities to locate the missing sailor.

About two thirds of ships that have been attacked since the start of the war in Iran have sustained only minor damage and were able to continue to their journeys, according to an analysis of U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center warnings. Most of the rest have been salvaged by vessels that towed them away, though last month two vessels sank. There have been a small number of reported incidents in recent weeks of Iranians targeting salvage vessels.

Martin Kelly, the chief executive officer of Orbital Risk Intelligence, a maritime risk firm, said he believes that Iran’s aim is to stop ships from passing through the strait. He did not think their intention was to harm rescuers, but to ensure that ships could not be salvaged. This raises insurance costs and could serve as a deterrent to shipowners.

“The longer the ship is on fire, the higher the cost of salvage,” he said.

Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up considerably since the early months of the war, in large part because the U.S. military has run an extensive operation to shield vessels from Iranian drone and missile attacks. But oil exports through the strait have not fully recovered to prewar levels.

Similarly, global oil prices are higher than they were before the start of the war, though they are down from recent highs. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, was around $93 a barrel on Thursday — down more than $20 a barrel since late October — as global supply finally caught up with demand. Even as more oil flows from the Middle East, the higher prices have pushed businesses and consumers to find ways to use less fuel.

The United States has carried out intermittent strikes on Iran, including this week, as peace talks have stalled. Iran has attacked fewer ships this month than in October, the most dangerous month since the start of the war, in which more than 38 attacks took place.

Iran’s neighbors in the Persian Gulf also face heightened threats. Kuwait and Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf, said on Wednesday that they had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks. The attack on Kuwait, which Iranian state media said had been aimed at U.S. air defense systems and missile launch platforms, was the first Iranian offensive against the country in about two months. Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, has reported several attacks since Friday.

Vivian Nereim contributed reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

item.title: ‘Did A.I. Break the Internet?’ and Other Things We’ve Worried About This Week
item.description:
Hosted by Rachel Abrams

Featuring Karoun DemirjianDustin Volz and Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Produced by Jack D’IsidoroChris Benderev and Eric Krupke

Edited by M.J. Davis Lin and Michael Benoist

item.title: Russia’s Takeover of Japan Tobacco Units Deals $8.6 Billion Blow
item.description:
Russia has taken over management of Japan Tobacco’s local operations, dealing a multibillion-dollar blow to a cigarette maker one-third owned by the Japanese government, in the latest escalation of President Vladimir Putin’s campaign to seize foreign businesses’ Russian assets.

On Thursday, Japan Tobacco said the seizure would force it to book a loss of roughly $8.6 billion for the Russian business this year, pushing the company into the red for the full year.

Mr. Putin issued decrees two weeks ago placing Japan Tobacco’s Russian subsidiaries under the temporary management of a local company. The move is particularly striking given the Japanese government’s substantial stake in the cigarette maker and underscores the rapid deterioration in relations between Moscow and Tokyo in recent months.

Japan Tobacco, which sells Camel and Winston cigarettes internationally, traces its origins to a national tobacco monopoly established by Japan’s Finance Ministry in 1898. Even after the company went public a century later, the ministry retained a majority stake for more than a decade before gradually reducing its holdings to one-third, the current legally mandated minimum.

Japan has formally protested Russia’s actions, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters earlier this month. Japan Tobacco said Thursday that it would “aim to maintain local business operations,” adding that the loss does not mean it planned to sell, relinquish or withdraw from the Russian unit. It said it would take “all available measures” to fulfill responsibilities to stakeholders and protect its rights and assets.

Japan Tobacco has operated in Russia for more than a quarter-century and has become the country’s largest tobacco company by sales volume. Roughly 10 percent of Japan Tobacco’s sales come from the Russian units. It employs roughly 4,000 people there, according to a company spokesman. Its shares have fallen more than 20 percent over the past month.

The seizure is part of a broader push by Mr. Putin to wrest Russian assets from companies based in countries Moscow considers unfriendly. In recent months, he has also targeted the local operations of Swiss food giant Nestlé as well as French and German grocery chains.

Japan joined international sanctions against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But the two countries maintained some economic ties, including through a joint venture in the Sakhalin-2 liquefied natural gas and oil project in Russia’s Far East.

More recently, Mr. Putin has intensified pressure on Japan in what analysts say may be an effort to pressure Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a foreign policy hawk, while rallying nationalist sentiment at home.

In August, Mr. Putin visited a disputed island seized from Japan at the end of World War II, drawing a rebuke from Ms. Takaichi. Two months later, Russia detained a Japanese journalist, accusing him of gathering intelligence about the country’s military capabilities.

Despite the tensions, Ms. Takaichi and Mr. Putin spoke for about 30 minutes on Wednesday evening at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. It was the first conversation between the two countries’ leaders since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Ms. Takaichi told reporters Thursday that she had raised concerns about “the cases of Japanese nationals being detained and the treatment of Japanese companies.” The two leaders agreed to maintain direct communication, she said, calling that “the biggest progress.”

item.title: Mamdani, Musk, Altman, Lagarde, A.I. and Other DealBook Summit Highlights
item.description:
Andrew here. Wednesday’s DealBook Summit was another huge day of headlines. Thanks to everyone who joined us in person and online. We’ve got all of the highlights below.

In the coming days, we’ll send a special series of newsletters that take you deeper into what was said, and delve into the insights, trends and predictions.

The upside and risk of artificial intelligence. America’s shifting politics and what it means for businesses and global trade. The continued fallout from Jensen Huang’s ouster. These topics and more dominated the discussions on Wednesday at the DealBook Summit.

Over the course of the day, speakers, including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Satya Nadella of Microsoft, dug into the challenges of scaling A.I. and keeping it safe. (Polymarket’s C.E.O., Shayne Coplan, raised eyebrows when he told Andrew that he had A.I. agents trading on his laptop in his green room as he spoke.) Discussions with speakers including Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York touched on their relationships with President Trump before and since Election Day.

Elon Musk surprised many when he described himself as “not MAGA,” and expressed regret for his record-breaking spending spree on Republican candidates after many floundered in the midterm elections.

Watch Andrew’s conversations here and catch up on all of The Times’s coverage here.

Here are some key themes.

Is the recent tech-stock sell-off a blip, or a sign that the A.I. industry is doomed to run out of steam? That was the big question that Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, addressed to kick off the event. She warned that while growth in A.I. had helped keep the global economy resilient, it might not end well. There is “a very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually,” she said.

On the flip side, Altman, the C.E.O. of OpenAI, an A.I. powerhouse expected to go public as soon as next year, downplayed the “ups and downs of valuations.” Overall, he said, the “trend is going to be strong.”

The debate took on extra emphasis as Anthropic priced a record-setting I.P.O. valuing the giant at more than $1.5 trillion. Its shares are set to begin trading on Thursday.

Beyond the financial fears around how fast the A.I. industry is growing is a fear of how powerful the technology itself has become. Greg Brockman, a founder at OpenAI and its president, said A.I. safety had become a bigger conversation (and focus at his company) as models became more capable.

“Models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new,” he said. “And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift.”

Both he and Altman stressed the need for humans to retain tight control over the technology. Nadella of Microsoft, for one, sounded skeptical that so-called alignment — the science of teaching A.I. to broadly follow human preferences and instructions — is fully possible.

Palmer Luckey, a founder of the defense contractor Anduril Industries, sees a potential dark cloud, however. He said he believed that the recent wave of tech outages affecting airlines, banks and our digital lives had an A.I. angle. He blamed tech outages on attackers using A.I. tools to target outdated infrastructure.

“As of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast-moving in using technology,” he said, “and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.”

Mamdani, the mayor of New York City and a democratic socialist, explained a bit about how he maintains an amicable relationship with Trump. He said the key to dealing with the president was “to focus on any possible area of commonality — and the reason for that is the stakes are so immense.”

One example: He said he had called the president to plead his case, asking for a relaxation of regulations to help the city’s bodegas and small retailers meet new federal food-stocking rules.

Carney, the Canadian prime minister, who met with Trump earlier in the day on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, has found negotiations on the countries’ trade spat progressing slower than he would like. But he also offered a contrasting view. In certain settings, Trump comes across as personable and engaged.

“He listens a lot more in private,” Carney said. “I mean, he’s interested, genuinely, in your opinion, and it’s a reasonably direct conversation.” Even so, Canada is advancing trade ties with China while talks with the Trump administration remain stalled over the tit-for-tat tariff war.

Governance watchdogs have long called into question business figures’ close ties to the president and his family — an issue that could draw serious scrutiny from a Democrat-controlled congress.

David Ellison, the C.E.O. of Skydance, could be one under the political microscope. In conversation with Andrew, Ellison took on issues as big as press freedom and as small as “Rush Hour 4.” Skydance’s decision to greenlight production of that film was for creative and commercial reasons, Ellison said, not because the studio was pressured to do so by Trump, who was previously reported to have requested that the studio revive the franchise.

Ellison’s media conglomerate, Paramount Skydance, was born out of a mega-merger with Warner Bros. after the Justice Department in June shuttered its investigation into the deal. Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, has a close relationship with Trump.

“We’ve been fortunate enough to be able to work closely with this administration,” Ellison said. But, he added, “when we started the Paramount deal, that was under the Biden administration,” with whom “we were working very closely.”

Later in the day, Coplan of Polymarket defended his company’s ties to Donald Trump Jr., the president’s elder son — who’s an investor in the company via his venture firm 1789 Capital — saying the relationship was “heavily overblown.”

The tech bosses on the agenda — including Altman of OpenAI and Luckey of Anduril — all expressed empathy toward Huang’s predicament after his ouster last week from Nvidia amid reports of his affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials determined to be a Chinese asset.

Some in the Trump administration have suggested Nvidia’s parting with Huang, who has said he would like a shot to return to the chip-making giant, is the right move. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that the company needed a “dramatic shake-up” — widely interpreted as a call for new blood to run Nvidia.

Tech leaders have had kinder words. Altman told Andrew: “I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

Musk, like others in Silicon Valley, said Huang was irreplaceable.

“Let’s say you’re the Chicago Bulls, middle of your second season, and you’ve got a winning streak that’s just going to happen, and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team,” Musk, the C.E.O. of SpaceX and Tesla, said, adding that this “doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me.”

Anthropic completes its blockbuster I.P.O., lifting tech stocks. The artificial intelligence lab sold $81.3 billion of its stock in the largest ever public listing. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, priced its shares at $83, above the preliminary range of $70 to $78, giving the company an initial valuation of about $1.5 trillion. A strong trading debut could alleviate some A.I. bubble fears.

Wall Street’s mega financing for Nvidia reportedly hasn’t been deployed. Investors and Silicon Valley were buzzing over the news this summer that the A.I. bellwether Nvidia had secured $500 billion in pledges from Apollo Global Management, Blackstone and others to help fund some Nvidia customers’ chip purchases. No capital has changed hands so far, however, and now some investors think it will fall short of expectations, The Wall Street Journal reports, citing unnamed sources.

President Trump meets with the leaders of China and Russia. Trump greeted Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, warmly before a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. A commitment to increase the production and supply of petroleum was among the points agreed to, according to a text of a joint statement released by Russia.

The Fed weighs more interest rate increases. Central bank officials predicted at their meeting last month that they would need to raise the Fed’s benchmark lending rate to combat inflation. The futures market on Thursday was signaling three rate increases over the next year.

Christine Lagarde: “The rest of the world is looking at the United States thinking institutions can actually hold — in spite of whatever happens.”

The departing president of the European Central Bank said that there were signs that democracy was alive and well in the United States again, in a much more positive assessment than she had earlier this year, when she described the country as acting strangely and undermining trust with its allies.

Mark Carney: “It should have been done six months ago, but we’re not going to sign something that doesn’t make sense for Canada.”

The prime minister of Canada commented on the recently revived trade talks between his country and the United States. While Washington has backed off on some minor issues, there’s no sign of a breakthrough on critical issues including the tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, auto and aluminum exports.

Hailey Bieber: “It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face — they make your lips bigger, your nose smaller.”

Bieber has used social media — where she has nearly 60 million Instagram followers and almost 20 million on TikTok — to great success with her beauty brand, Rhode, which was sold last year for at least $800 million. But she is also fully aware of the perils of the technology, which can be addictive and can make her feel insecure. “But it’s part of the world we’re living in — it’s not going anywhere,” she added.

Palmer Luckey: “Everyone already knows we need more killer robots.”

Luckey, a founder of the defense tech company Anduril Industries, said that his role in discussions with the military and the government about the future of war was to point out things that they may not have considered. As new as autonomous warfare may seem to many, killer robots are old news to Luckey and to many steeped in defense at this point. What Luckey tries to do is suggest ideas that people in the public sector may not have considered, such as how tech might be used to control the weather in the context of war.

Vlad Tenev: “I don’t want to be the one telling you that you can’t trade something.”

Tenev, the C.E.O. of Robinhood — speaking alongside the Nasdaq chief Adena Friedman and the Polymarket founder Shayne Coplan — weighed in on a debate about the blurry line between investing and gambling. He argued that regular traders should have access to the same investment opportunities available to the ultrawealthy.

Sam Altman: “We’re not going to be able to make everybody happy.”

OpenAI’s C.E.O. appeared with the company’s president, Greg Brockman, and discussed how OpenAI had to balance addressing artificial intelligence safety issues with continuing progress on A.I. development. And while its rival Anthropic is set to begin trading on Thursday, OpenAI’s I.P.O. future is thought to be in the cards next year. Altman said on Wednesday that the public listing would come “at some point.”

Satya Nadella: Founders are “singular, but they’re not gods.”

Microsoft’s C.E.O. said that he had confidence in the leaders of Nvidia and that the company could still succeed without its co-founder, Jensen Huang, at the helm. Founders are incredible, he said, because they have created something out of nothing. But he made the case that founders should be proud when their companies thrive beyond their tenure; otherwise, what did they build?

Zohran Mamdani: “Comrades. It’s great to be here at the largest D.S.A. meeting Lincoln Center has ever seen.”

The mayor of New York City calls the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America his political home, but he is also famously amiable and eager to present himself as willing to engage with people from across the political spectrum, including President Trump. On Wednesday, the first words he uttered were clearly meant to disarm the crowd, many of whom chuckled in response.

David Ellison: “If there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege.”Ellison discussed Elon Musk’s investment in Paramount. He left the door open to future collaboration with Musk amid speculation that Starlink might offer Paramount content on its service, which is used by a number of airlines.

Elon Musk: “I’m not MAGA”The billionaire, who gave nearly $500 million to back Republican candidates in the midterm elections, sought to play down his ties to the party after a drubbing at the polls. Musk said he felt “pretty foolish” about spending so much “and not seeing much for it.” There are “positives and negatives in both” political parties, he added.

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.description:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant, will begin trading on the stock market later Thursday, a bellwether debut for a major A.I. company amid a global technology race and boom some have cautioned could become a bubble.

The company completed its initial public offering as the world’s largest stock market debut, a testament to investors’ belief in the A.I. giant’s business prowess, valuing the company at more than $1.5 trillion. Anthropic’s shares will begin trading on Thursday on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Anthropic’s offering is the first time that public market investors will have the chance to invest in one of the A.I. industry’s “frontier labs,” which are developing the core models underlying the boom. The company’s offering prospectus showed a fast-growing business alongside a narrative of future growth and abundance, including curing diseases and expanding economic prosperity. Revenue soared to $33 billion in the first nine months of the year from $41 million in 2023.

The company’s offering topped that of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which in June raised a then record-breaking $75 billion at a higher valuation: $1.77 trillion. Read more ›

Power play: Anthropic is going public partly because its voracious demand for computing power is hugely expensive. The company has issued convertible debt to finance some of the infrastructure it needs, like chips, data centers and electricity. item.title: When will Anthropic shares start trading?
item.description:
The U.S. stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, but don’t expect shares of Anthropic to begin trading right away.

Delaying the start of trading in shares in a newly public company is part of an elaborate effort to ensure that the stock’s introduction into the market goes as smoothly as possible.

A key part of that is deciding at what price Anthropic should begin trading.

Bankers will spend Thursday morning trying to assess from traders how much demand there is to sell and buy Anthropic shares at various prices. They are looking for an “equilibrium” price: the price at which there is generally the same amount of sellers as buyers.

The goal is to make sure that the company’s shares are relatively stable when they begin to trade. Ideally, underwriters hope they will rise gradually throughout the trading day. Ultimately, the price bankers land on for the opening trade could be below, above or the same as the $83-a-share initial public offering price that was determined on Wednesday night.

For such a large offering as Anthropic, it could take hours for the process to play out before the trading can start.

Several previous high-profile listings were in the late morning: Shares of Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant, began trading at 11:53 a.m. on Sept. 19, 2014; and shares of Twitter began trading a little before 11 a.m. on Nov. 7, 2013. Shares of SpaceX started trading just before noon on June 12.

item.title: How Anthropic’s Dario Amodei thinks about A.I.
item.description:
Even before he earned his doctorate in physics from Princeton two decades ago, Dario Amodei had made a habit of soaking up information about artificial intelligence, its prospects, its risks and its responsibility to humanity.

He became absorbed in obscure blogs where writers discussed A.I.’s potential to wipe out humanity. He delved into the online forums where intellectuals debated how to make the most money for philanthropy.

One night in 2007, he regaled a friend with his thoughts on a book that predicted that artificial intelligence would eventually surpass the human brain — a milestone that Dr. Amodei told his friend could happen within their lifetimes.

These books, blogs and online communities have influenced Dr. Amodei to this day, according to interviews with more than two dozen of his classmates, friends, teachers and colleagues. They help explain the ideas that drive the 43-year-old chief executive of Anthropic, a company that is set to conduct one of the world’s largest public listings this month, and offer an understanding of how the man at the forefront of the A.I. revolution actually thinks about A.I.

item.title: China Is Shut Out of a Blockbuster Public Offering Once Again
item.description:
It was the biggest initial public offering in history and investors from China and Hong Kong were left out.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company and maker of the Claude chatbot, excluded investment from Chinese and Hong Kong firms from buying its shares in advance of the I.P.O., according to three people with knowledge of the decision, who asked not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

A representative for Anthropic declined to comment, and the reason for not accepting investments from the region was not clear. But it follows a move by the Trump administration to keep artificial intelligence out of China’s reach. Both Washington and Beijing are drawing red lines around their homegrown technology as they compete for supremacy in A.I.

It also follows a similar move by SpaceX and its bankers to shut out China from its blockbuster public offering in July. OpenAI, another leading A.I. company, is expected to bar Chinese investors from its eventual public offering. OpenAI has already barred Chinese investors from participating in private fund-raising. All three companies have counted the U.S. government as a client.

The news that Anthropic would bar Chinese investors was reported earlier by Bloomberg.

President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met on Thursday at the APEC meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Mr. Xi called on members to build an “open ecosystem” for technology.

Both Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi are trying to inject some stability — and a little bonhomie — into an increasingly rocky economic relationship between the world’s two biggest economies. But their governments continue to build fortresses around trade, technology and capital.

Hours before Mr. Trump arrived in Asia to attend meetings with regional leaders, his administration moved to restrict China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips. In response, China warned it could hit back, saying “if the U.S. persists, China will take countermeasures.”

“China is deeply concerned about — and firmly opposes — a series of recent economic and trade restrictive measures taken by the U.S. against China,” a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday.

China experts warned that the new A.I. rule, the latest in a series of escalatory moves from both sides, will make it harder for both Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump to come to any meaningful agreement to de-escalate rising conflict between the world’s biggest economies.

item.title: Should You Invest in Anthropic? Here’s What to Consider.
item.description:
Buying into Anthropic doesn’t feel like your typical single-stock bet.

Unlike many initial public offering disclosure forms, this one won’t put you to sleep — but it may drive you to reach for a Xanax.

The artificial intelligence company, which on Thursday was the first A.I. lab to go public, explains the singular wager its investors are making in its prospectus, the regulatory filing that describes a new company’s business strategy, prospects and risks.

It lays out its great promise (curing diseases like cancer, developing drugs and other revolutionary innovations) and its most perilous downsides, among them “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

The notion of existential risk hasn’t prevented investors from piling into the shares of the company, valued at $1.5 trillion, which released roughly 6 percent of its shares overall to the public. Demand was far higher: The stock was priced at $83 a share, above its original target of $70 to $78, and opened trading at $111.50, a 34 percent jump.

Placing a significant portion of your wealth on a single stock is never a good idea, but there’s always the temptation to buy something when a shiny new offering comes along. Research still shows that keeping a diversified mix of stocks and bonds over the long-term is the best bet you can make.

But if you’re considering Anthropic, here are several questions to ask yourself first.

If you hold U.S. stock index funds, you’re probably already investing in A.I. — and you’re arguably even overexposed. About 35 percent of the holdings that the Morningstar Total Stock Index tracks, for example, are directly related to some type of A.I. play, according to Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer of Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity.

That includes so-called hyperscalers, or companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta that operate vast computing and data infrastructure; chip suppliers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices; among other categories.

Another proxy is to look at how much money your funds have allocated to the so-called Magnificent Seven, or the seven largest tech holdings, some of which have invested in Anthropic or are otherwise interconnected to the industry. This group accounts for more than a quarter of U.S. stock index funds that track the entire market, and more than a third of the S&P 500. This collection also drove 46 percent of the S&P 500’s overall return in 2025, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and 55 percent in 2024, underscoring just how much they’re buoying overall performance.

Many U.S. stock index fund investors will also automatically own Anthropic stock before too long, as soon as the next week, though the initial amount will be small. Index funds try to reflect the entire stock market — so many of them will incorporate Anthropic based on the amount of shares that are publicly available.

Anthropic’s stock will initially account for an estimated 0.05 percent to 0.15 percent of the Vanguard Total Stock Market, for example, though that is likely to grow over time.

Other index funds don’t move as quickly. Funds that track the S&P 500 Index, for example, generally follow a different set of rules, which has a 12-month waiting period but also requires companies to meet profitability hurdles.

There may also be other companies that are helped (or hurt) by A.I., just as different businesses were revolutionized by the internet.

“If you look 20 years later, the companies that benefit the most from the internet worlds are something like a Home Depot or a Walmart,” Mr. Comegys added, which helped improve supply chains and sales.

Financial journalists are prohibited from investing in companies we write about. The last time I can remember buying an individual stock — Krispy Kreme! — was not long after the first tech boom. That purchase felt like an old-fashioned, Warren Buffett brand of capitalism — a company you could generally understand, and the big risk was that the chain would grow too fast.

How much can any average person truly understand about a company as complex as Anthropic, along with its founders? When you make a single bet, you’re also betting on the company’s leaders. After Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence became public this month, its stock plummeted. Since its peak in October, the company has given up a third, or $2 trillion, of its market value.

There’s a lot we won’t know, even if our policymakers demand more transparency and regulation.

In September, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI said he resigned from Anthropic because he felt “neither company is acting responsibly.”

One of Anthropic’s billionaire founders recently tried to convince religious scholars that Claude could become conscious.

It’s a lot to process.

Stocks that make splashy debuts can be disappointing performers, at least for a while. Investors are essentially paying $42 for each dollar of Anthropic’s revenue. Similar companies that cost more than $40 for each dollar of revenue have underperformed the broader market in the three years after their I.P.O., even for investors who bought at the offer price, according to an analysis by Jay Ritter, an I.P.O. expert at the University of Florida. (New technology offerings overall, however, tended to outperform non-tech I.P.O.s during that same time period.)

“With Anthropic, and for that matter, SpaceX,” he said, “the valuations are reflecting very optimistic assumptions.” He added, “This time could be different, because these are companies, Anthropic in particular, with game-changing technology that’s not easy to duplicate.”

Several brokerage firms — Charles Schwab, E*Trade, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi and others — had access to a portion of the initial shares, and were offering customers the chance to acquire them at the I.P.O. price. But there were no guarantees that all customers who expressed interest would receive them.

Each firm had different rules on how they would be allocated. At Fidelity and Schwab, for example, customers needed to have at least $25,000 and $50,000 in assets, respectively, to participate.

Many financial planners have said it’s perfectly fine to take a small portion of your overall stock portfolio, say 5 percent, for play money and placing bets — as long as the rest of your savings remains diversified and thoughtfully positioned to meet specific longer-term goals, whether for retirement or college.

Having some play money can be wise — especially if it leaves you less tempted to make changes elsewhere, allowing compounding to work its magic over time.

item.title: America’s Biggest Retailers Sell Affordability This Holiday Season
item.description:
Shoppers are seeking out lower prices and ways to cut costs as they manage tight household budgets. They’re stocking up on essential items, and doing more home repairs.

Affordability is paramount for Americans this holiday season, and the nation’s largest retailers are selling value above all to lure consumers struggling with higher costs in an uncertain economy.

Several retailers have cut prices on thousands of items, rolled out low-price gift sections, emphasized cheaper private-label goods and started holiday promotions earlier than usual.

John Furner, the chief executive of Walmart, told investors Thursday that its customers are “stable, resilient” as the holiday season begins. Almost half of Americans said their finances are their top source of stress as they buy gifts and host family, according to Walmart.

“I think we are in good shape in terms of customer response, but we will always do whatever we can to continue to lower prices as we look ahead,” Mr. Furner said.

That strategy was echoed by several major retailers across the country, reflecting broader concerns about the U.S. economy and an affordability crisis. The war in Iran has driven up gas prices, tariffs have pushed up inflation in consumer goods and high interest rates have made loans more expensive.

”Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend,” Cara Sylvester, the chief merchandising officer of Target, told investors on a call this week. “That is exactly how we have approached this holiday season.”

Despite the economic pressures, consumers are still expected to spend big. The National Retail Federation, a trade association, said it expects retail sales in the United States over the holiday season will grow 4.2 percent to over $1 trillion this year. Holiday sales grew 3.1 percent last year.

“This year’s forecast reflects our confidence that consumers will prioritize the holiday season even as they remain mindful of their budgets,” Matthew Shay, the group’s chief executive, said in a statement.

On Thursday, Walmart raised its outlook for the full fiscal year and said that it had seen shoppers pressured throughout the year, especially in April and June. At the end of its most recent quarter, the company had lowered prices on 7,700 items.

Target, in the midst of a turnaround effort, posted its strongest sales growth in more than five years and raised its guidance. Michael Fiddelke, its chief executive, told investors that the company has made “fundamental changes to how we build and run the business.”

“We know affordability remains top of mind for busy families, which is why it is top of mind for us as well,” Mr. Fiddelke said.

Off-price retailers are also seeing more American consumers as they search for the best deals. TJX, which owns TJ Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods, raised its full-year sales outlook and said it expects that momentum to build for its heavily discounted apparel and household products.

“We have become such the gifting destination, I think not just in the off-price world, but in all retail,” Ernie Herrman, the chief executive of TJX, said on a call with analysts.

The diligence that Americans have shown when shopping for consumer goods has extended to spending on their homes. Homeowners aren’t splurging on renovations like they used to. High interest rates have stalled the housing market for years, and inflationary pressures have led homeowners to put off big remodeling projects in favor of small fixes and upgrades.

Home Depot and Lowe’s, the largest home improvement retailers in the United States, each reported earnings results this week that were boosted by healthy repair businesses and robust sales of appliances, even as they manage higher costs for fuel, resin and metals brought on by the war in Iran.

Bill Boltz, the executive vice president of merchandising at Lowe’s, said on a call on Wednesday that repairs have been the “dominant occasion” for the professional contractors who shop at the stores.

The home improvement industry refers to these consumers as “duress customers”: those who have no choice but to spend money to repair or replace broken appliances immediately to keep their daily lives running smoothly.

“One-hundred-thousand appliances break every day,” Mr. Boltz said, adding that the company is able to handle same-day and next-day orders to “handle that duress customer.”

Lowe’s raised its revenue forecast for the full year; its comparable sales grew 1.8 percent in its most recent quarter. Company executives said demand for its offerings have improved.

Home Depot posted its fastest sales growth in four years, up 4.6 percent in its most recent quarter, though its profit margins compressed. Appliances were a key driver for big-ticket sales.

“Maintenance and repair is certainly driving our business,” Billy Bastek, the executive vice president of merchandising at Home Depot, told investors. “We feel really good about the underlying demand and what we can control, and, candidly, the share that we are taking along the way.”

Still, Richard McPhail, the company’s incoming chief executive, acknowledged the tough economic environment he will face on Monday, when he starts the job.

“Housing turnover hasn’t moved in four years now,” Mr. McPhail told investors. “It is pressure out there.”

item.title: Food Delivery Is Making a Killing on Grand Theft Auto
item.description:
While Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI, were fortifying themselves with food from fictional restaurant chains like Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell, real-life businesses were cashing in Thursday on the real-life players who were too intent on playing the game to cook for themselves.

“It’s all hands on deck,” said Frank Lucido, co-owner of Frankie & Joe’s Pizza in Boca Raton, Fla., hours after the game’s midnight release. “It’s going to be a really big one tonight.”

DoorDash reported that from 9 p.m. on Wednesday to 2 a.m. on Thursday, its orders in Miami — where the game is set — were up by 25 percent over a typical Wednesday night, with Philadelphia, Detroit and Atlanta also seeing double-digit increases. Its overall sales of energy drinks were up by more than 20 percent, while orders for pizza, burgers, fries and chips rose more than 10 percent.

Uber Eats said that overnight, its Miami sales were 30 percent higher than on the last two Thursdays. The company said it saw big spikes in sales of specific snacks and drinks commonly associated with gamers: orders for Red Bull Watermelon were up by 95 percent, Totino’s Pizza Rolls by 54 percent and Ghost Sour Strips by 46 percent.

At Frankie & Joe’s Pizza, before the game was released, Mr. Lucido made sure the store was fully staffed, ensured that his two best pizzaiolos would be working and doubled the amount of dough ready to slide into the oven, expecting that orders would really start picking up around 2 p.m. on Thursday.

He said he was considering keeping the restaurant open till midnight, rather than the usual 11 p.m. closing time, if the traffic warranted it. The store is also offering 20 percent discounts on delivery orders using the in-app code GTA.

“This is going to be gigantic, this game,” he said. “There’s going to be lots of young guys and middle-aged guys who are going to be staying home and playing the game.”

At the Pizza Box in Dearborn Heights, Mich., the owner, Rodney Barro, told his staff two weeks ago that everyone had to work the day of the game’s release. He also redecorated the store’s exterior to mimic the Grand Theft Auto aesthetic, and offered a release-day $6 sale on several menu items.

He expected that the store would double its usual Thursday sales. The only person he allowed to stay home was his 14-year-old gamer son. “I gave him the day off from school — he’s ‘sick,’” Mr. Barro said, laughing.

It’s not just the mom-and-pops that were anticipating bigger sales. On Wednesday, McDonald’s introduced a new service that lets players order delivery right on Discord, the communication platform most popular with gamers. Popeyes added a limited-edition Spice City sandwich inspired by Vice City, Grand Theft Auto’s version of Miami.

In the real-world Miami, Rockstar Games — the company that produced Grand Theft Auto — partnered with the local hamburger chain Skinny Louie to redecorate locations inside the Kaseya Center as Burger Shot stalls, and opened a Cluckin’ Bell chicken store inside the arena.

Uber Eats has rolled out promo codes and discounts for food, drinks and products often at the center of gaming culture — from Red Bulls delivered from 7-Eleven to HDMI cables from Best Buy and GameStop.

“We want Uber Eats to be there for fans during the biggest moment in gaming, with everything from gaming accessories and groceries to their favorite meal on launch day,” said Andrew Macdonald, the president and chief operating officer of Uber. “We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game.”

Similarly, DoorDash is offering partner discounts with Wendy’s and the Cheesecake Factory. “GTA 6 is more than a game launch. It’s a cultural moment that fans have been waiting years for,” Gina Igwe, vice president of brand, creative and consumer marketing at DoorDash, wrote in an email.

For gamers, especially on release days, food delivery can be vital, said Ryan Morrison, the agent of Félix Lengyel (better known as xQc), who is widely recognized as the most-watched Grand Theft Auto streamer.

“It’s a demand of their time and attention unlike anything else, and that’s why so many live and die by online delivery platforms like DoorDash or Uber Eats,” Mr. Morrison said in an email. “Felix uses it constantly to feed both him and his girlfriend during their marathon streams each day, and easily spends six figures a year doing so.”

Mr. Morrison said that for big occasions like the Grand Theft Auto VI release, Mr. Lengyel needs to stream constantly for 18 hours or longer. “A nutritionist wouldn’t be happy with most orders, as it’s a lot of fast food or things he can eat quickly rather than have to make a whole meal out of,” Mr. Morrison said.

Neil Saunders, managing director of the retail division for the consumer research analysis firm Global Data, said he expected the spike in all food deliveries to be around 20 percent, a notable rise but not to the level of the Super Bowl, which he estimated creates a 27 to 35 percent jump in demand.

“Not everyone is a gamer, and not all gamers necessarily will play the whole night,” he said. “It will probably trend into the weekend and peter out next week as most have gotten their fix of the new game. I would say it’s more like the levels you would see at college towns during the exams — that’s the parallel.”

Mr. Saunders also said grocery stores might see slower sales, except for snack foods and ready-to-eat meals.And he didn’t expect delivery apps to crash because of high volume, despite the issues plaguing so many digital platforms in recent days.

“I don’t think it’s a system-collapsing event,” he said. “You might see longer wait times and lower driver availability.”

Still, restaurants that primarily cater to walk-in customers were wary. Ilyass Berraho, the owner of Pizzeria Padrino in Columbus, Ohio, which caters mostly to a late-night crowd of Ohio State University students, said he was already seeing such a troubling slowdown in walk-in sales the night of the game’s release that he closed earlier than usual, at around 2:20 a.m.

“It was dead outside,” he said, estimating that walk-in sales were half of the usual, though delivery orders were up about 20 percent. “I know a lot of people are talking about G.T.A., and a lot of students are getting ready for it — I don’t know. Is that the G.T.A. effect?”

Ultimately, how the food-delivery business fares with the Grand Theft Auto release may come down to how indulgent gamers’ families are toward their latest obsession. That’s something Chris Hassan, a 41-year-old American travel writer living in Rio de Janeiro, is counting on.

“Haha,” he texted. “I’m hoping my wife will be sympathetic and take over meal duties for the weekend.”

item.title: JPMorgan Chase Customer Data Is Exposed in Latest Hack
item.description:
Hackers stole reams of customer data belonging to JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard, the companies said on Thursday, the latest in a string of nerve-rattling cybersecurity incidents.

The data included names, email addresses and phone numbers for some Chase customers, as well as similar information from Mastercard and Visa credit card holders. It was serious enough that JPMorgan overnight notified officials at the White House of the breach, according to two people familiar with the outreach who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

None of the three financial institutions would specify how many customers were impacted, although Mastercard said it was a “small subset of cardholders.” The companies said the theft was the result of hackers breaching a vendor that worked for them.

JPMorgan was asked to pay a ransom to the hackers, and declined to do so, the two people said.

In a statement, a JPMorgan spokesman said “the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by vendors that was limited to some customer names, email addresses and a small amount of other public information.”

Mastercard said the incident exposed “non-payments information.” Visa blamed “a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific” and said “no payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

Cybersecurity and the technological patchwork that holds it all together have become hot topics in the wake of last week’s F.A.A. ground stop and a series of tech outages at major U.S. companies. This week, some Chase banking services were briefly disrupted, which the company blamed on a “software bug.”

Even access to nonsensitive customer information can be helpful to hackers. They can use the data to set up “phishing” operations in which scammers pretend to be representatives of trusted companies, such as banks, and trick individuals into transferring funds or disclosing personal data.
